Mathematical optimization

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 75k Articles: 1k
Mathematical optimization turns a preference into a precise question: among the allowed decisions, which gives the best outcome? A model separates the objective function, which measures quality, from the optimization constraints, which determine the feasible set. This language unifies finding a cheap plan for a transportation problem, efficient scheduling, or an accurate model in linear regression. The separation is useful because changing a preference and changing what is possible are different modeling decisions. See Boyd and Vandenberghe, introductory optimization models.
For an objective function f:F→R, a maximization problem asks for a feasible point z∗​ satisfying f(z∗​)≥f(z) for every z∈F; a minimization problem reverses the inequality. This is a global extremum. A local maximum or local minimum compares only nearby feasible points, so finding one does not settle the global question.
Consider allocating ten units between two complementary inputs:
maxxysubject to x+y=10,x,y≥0.
(1)
The budget constraint forces a tradeoff: an extra unit of x costs a unit of y. The best allocation is (5,5), with objective function value 25. Without the budget constraint, x=y=t gives xy=t2→∞: there is no global maximum. Constrained optimization can therefore have a finite answer even when the corresponding problem with fewer optimization constraints does not. Its beauty is that geometry, calculus, and an arithmetic-geometric mean inequality can certify the same answer.

Dinkelbach's algorithm

For maximizing A(x)/B(x) with B(x)>0, repeatedly maximize A(x)−rB(x) and update r to the ratio at the selected maximizer. If the maximum difference is zero, r is the optimal ratio. Exact convergence claims require the relevant existence and regularity assumptions.

Constraint qualification

Words: 69
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
A constraint qualification is a regularity hypothesis on optimization constraints that guarantees a specified optimality or duality conclusion. For the necessity of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, an appropriate constraint qualification ensures that a local minimum admits suitable Lagrange multipliers; linear independence of the gradients of equality optimization constraints and active constraints is one sufficient hypothesis in KKT regularity at a local minimum.[ref] Slater's condition provides a different constraint qualification for convex optimization, yielding strong duality and dual attainment.[ref]

Scheduling

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Scheduling assigns jobs to processing resources and orders their execution subject to resource and precedence requirements. Objectives include completion time, lateness and throughput. In single-machine sequencing with all jobs mandatory, the total processing time is constant, but order-dependent setups can still change completion time. With parallel machines, machine allocation and sequencing jointly determine the parallel-machine makespan with sequence-dependent setups.

Parallel-machine makespan with sequence-dependent setups (Cmax​=maxr​Cr​)

Words: 79
Scheduling OurBigBook.com
Partition jobs between machines and choose an ordering on each machine. Machine r has load Cr​ equal to its processing times, initial setup and internal changeovers; the completion time of all jobs is the maximum of these loads. Minimize a variable Cmax​ subject to Cr​≤Cmax​ for every machine. Branch and bound can combine machine-assignment decisions with route bounds; heuristic moves relocate jobs between machines, swap jobs, and reorder blocks. Minimizing the sum of route costs alone does not generally minimize the makespan.

Objective function (f(x))

Words: 201
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
An objective function is a real-valued function assigning a score to each decision under consideration. An optimization problem seeks a feasible solution maximizing or minimizing this score. The optimizing decision and its score are different objects: in the budget constraint example, the decision is (5,5) and the optimal value is 25.
Choosing an objective function expresses what matters. With x+y=10 and x,y≥0, maximizing x+y makes every feasible point equally good; maximizing x selects (10,0); maximizing xy rewards balance. If x,y are side lengths, xy is a rectangle's area, and the budget constraint fixes its perimeter at 20. The same mathematics then says that a square encloses the largest area among these rectangles.
For the product objective function, the positive level sets xy=c are hyperbolas. Each collects decisions with identical scores. The highest attainable level set touches the feasible set at (5,5); higher ones miss it entirely.
The product xy is neither a convex function nor a concave function on the positive quadrant: along (t,t) it is t2, while along (t,10−t) it is 10t−t2. Yet its restriction to this feasible set is a strictly concave function. Thus the geometry of the allowed decisions can make an otherwise nonconcave maximization problem tractable. Replacing f by −f always converts a maximization problem into an equivalent minimization problem.

Project scheduling

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Project scheduling asks how quickly a collection of dependent activities can finish. Adding their durations usually overestimates the answer, because independent activities can run together; taking only the longest single activity usually underestimates it, because some activities must wait. The critical path method identifies the chain of dependencies that determines the finish time. Its simplest model assumes known, fixed durations, unlimited parallel processing, and precedence requirements saying that each predecessor must finish before its successor starts. These are the assumptions of the basic model in Hendrickson, Project Management for Construction, §10.2.
Represent each activity by a vertex of a finite Directed acyclic graph; an edge i→j means that activity j waits for activity i. Activity i runs without interruption for duration τi​≥0, starting at ti​≥0. The optimization constraints and project finish time are
tj​≥ti​+τi​(i→j),T=maxi​(ti​+τi​).
(2)
The objective function is to minimize T. All durations and start times use the same time unit, and the project starts at time zero. The Directed acyclic graph assumption allows a topological order in which every predecessor is processed first.
Consider this small, abstract project:
ActivityDurationImmediate predecessors
A3None
B2A
C4A
D2B and C
E3None
F1D and E
Activities A and E may start together. After A finishes, B and C may run together, but D must wait for both. F must similarly wait for both D and E: a merge means all incoming requirements must hold. This activity-as-vertex convention keeps durations on the activities and uses arrows only to express precedence.
Unlimited parallel processing is essential to the equality between the longest graph path duration and the optimal finish time. For example, two independent chains, each containing two activities of duration 3, have longest graph path duration 6. Two processors can finish both chains in 6, but one processor needs 12 because all four activities must run sequentially. Thus with limited resources the longest graph path still gives a lower bound, but it need not be achievable. Such resource requirements belong to the broader subject of scheduling.
// Target: mathematical-optimization.bigb

Critical path method

Words: 929 Articles: 3
Project scheduling OurBigBook.com
The critical path method calculates an earliest schedule, a latest schedule for a chosen finish time, and each activity's task float. A critical path is a start-to-finish graph path whose total duration is greatest. There can be several such graph paths, and every one constrains completion. In the six-activity project scheduling example, the critical graph path is A-C-D-F, of duration 3+4+2+1=10.
Add a zero-duration source s before every initial activity and a zero-duration sink z after every terminal activity. Give each edge i→j weight τi​, including zero weight on edges leaving s. This produces a weighted graph in which a graph path's weight counts every activity on it exactly once. The possible source-to-sink graph paths in our example, omitting the dummy endpoints, are A-B-D-F with weight 8, A-C-D-F with weight 10, and E-F with weight 4.
Every feasible schedule must accommodate each of these sequential chains. Consequently,
T≥maxP:s⇝z​∑i∈P∖{z}​τi​.
(3)
This bound applies to all source-to-sink graph paths, not just the one we happen to inspect. The critical path method attains the bound by setting each activity's earliest start Ei​ to the maximum of its predecessors' earliest finish times:
Es​=0,Ej​=maxi→j​(Ei​+τi​),T∗​=Ez​.
(4)
Evaluate this recurrence in a topological order, obtained by topological sorting. Each Ej​ satisfies every incoming optimization constraint, so these times form a feasible solution. The same recurrence calculates the greatest weight of a graph path from s to j; hence the feasible finish Ez​ matches the lower bound. This is dynamic programming on a Directed acyclic graph, rather than an enumeration of all graph paths. See Paul Johnson, Scheduling and longest paths, longest-path algorithm. The linear programming formulation and its certificate are developed in project scheduling duality and unit-flow certificate for project duration.
For our project scheduling example, EA​=EE​=0, EB​=EC​=3, and the two merges give
ED​=max(3+2,3+4)=7,EF​=max(7+2,0+3)=9.
(5)
F finishes at 10. All six activities are completed, even though E is absent from the critical graph path. Recording which predecessor attains each maximum lets us trace a critical graph path backward from the sink; retaining tied choices exposes multiple critical graph paths.
Now fix the project start at zero and the finish at T∗​=10. The latest starts Li​ come from a backward pass in reverse topological order:
Lz​=T∗​,Li​=mini→j​(Lj​−τi​).
(6)
Every activity must finish by the earliest of its successors' latest starts, explaining the minimum here. This gives LF​=9, LD​=7, LE​=6, LB​=5, LC​=3, and LA​=min(5−3,3−3)=0. These latest times themselves form a feasible solution finishing at 10. The backward calculation depends on the chosen finish time; a later deadline would give different latest times and task floats. The forward and backward passes are described in Olivier de Weck, MIT ESD.36 Lecture 2, slides 22–29.
ActivityEarliest start Ei​Earliest finish Ei​+τi​Latest start Li​Latest finish Li​+τi​Task float Li​−Ei​

Changing a duration can change which graph paths are critical. If B's duration becomes 4, A-B-D-F and A-C-D-F both take 10: there are two critical graph paths. Shortening C alone then cannot reduce the finish time, because the chain through B still takes 10. If B's duration instead becomes 5, the earliest starts of D and F become 8 and 10, and the finish becomes 11. A-B-D-F is now the unique critical graph path; C has task float 1 relative to that new optimal finish. These calculations show why the critical path method is useful for understanding where a duration change matters, even in a project containing many parallel activities.

Task float (TFi​=Li​−Ei​)

Words: 252
Critical path method OurBigBook.com
Task float, also called total float or task slack, measures an activity's available start-time delay relative to its earliest start, while allowing a feasible schedule that meets the fixed project finish. For earliest start Ei​, latest start Li​, and fixed duration τi​, it is
TFi​=Li​−Ei​=(Li​+τi​)−(Ei​+τi​).
(7)
In the six-activity project scheduling example with start zero and finish 10, B has task float 2 and E has task float 6. B can move from the interval [3,5] to [5,7], and E from [0,3] to [6,9], without changing D's or F's earliest starts. A, C, D, and F have zero task float. With the finish fixed to the optimal duration and the basic critical path method assumptions, zero task float identifies exactly the activities lying on at least one critical graph path. See Hendrickson, §10.4, Activity Float and Schedules.
Task float is not generally an independent allowance that can be spent separately on every activity. For a small example, let two duration-1 activities X then Y form one chain, running in parallel with a separate duration-4 activity. The optimal finish is 4. X has earliest/latest starts 0/2 and Y has earliest/latest starts 1/3, so each has task float 2. Delaying X to 2 forces Y to start at 3, using Y's allowance too. Choosing X at its latest start 2 and Y at its earliest start 1 violates precedence, although both chosen times lie inside their individual ranges. The optimization constraints still couple the decisions. Here B and E can both use their full task floats together because they lie on separate branches; that freedom must be checked from the Directed acyclic graph.

A feasible timetable with finish time T and a unit flow carried on a precedence path of total duration T certify optimality. Summing the inequalities tj​−ti​≥τi​ along that path proves every schedule needs at least T, while the timetable attains it.

Maximum and minimum

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Maxima and minima are extrema of a real-valued function. A global maximum of f on its domain D is a point x∗​ with f(x)≤f(x∗​) for every x∈D; a global minimum reverses the inequality. A local extremum requires the inequality only in a neighbourhood of the point within D. In constrained optimization, D is the feasible set, so an extremum is tested relative to the constraints rather than in every ambient direction. Thus a constrained local maximum or local minimum can occur at a boundary point without being an interior critical point.

Local extremum

Words: 38
Maximum and minimum OurBigBook.com
A local extremum of a real-valued function is either a local maximum or a local minimum, with comparisons restricted to a neighbourhood in its domain. A differentiable interior local extremum is a stationary point, but the converse can fail, as f(x)=x3 at zero shows.

Cobb–Douglas production function (f(K,L)=AKαLβ)

Words: 99
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
For positive constants A,α,β, a Cobb–Douglas production function describes output in terms of capital K and labour L. It is homogeneous of degree α+β. Simulated annealing

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Heuristic optimization OurBigBook.com
Simulated annealing accepts worse feasible solutions to escape a local minimum. Minimize an objective function E(x), analogous to energy. Effective temperature T>0 has the same units as E, absorbing the Boltzmann constant; it controls exploration, rather than a material's thermodynamic temperature.[ref]
Given current feasible point x, draw y from a proposal distribution q(x,y). For a symmetric proposal distribution, q(x,y)=q(y,x), use the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability
ΔE=E(y)−E(x),aT​(x,y)=min{1,exp(−ΔE/T)}.
(9)
Accept with this conditional probability; on rejection retain x. Every downhill or equal-cost proposal is accepted. Draw a fresh uniform random variable U on (0,1) and accept if U<aT​(x,y). The off-diagonal transition probability PT​(x,y)=q(x,y)aT​(x,y) includes proposing y.[ref]
For a maximization problem with objective function f, set E=−f: every improving proposed neighbor is accepted, and a worsening move of loss Δ=f(x)−f(y)>0 has conditional probability exp(−Δ/T) of acceptance, under the same symmetry assumption. Likelihood-power annealing uses precisely this sign convention for a log-likelihood. Retain the best feasible solution seen, since the current state can worsen even after a global minimum has been visited.
If the proposal distribution is asymmetric, use the full Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability, for q(x,y)>0,
aT​(x,y)=min{1,exp(−TE(y)−E(x)​)q(x,y)q(y,x)​}.
(10)
A missing reverse proposal gives zero acceptance. Even a downhill proposal need not be accepted with probability one in this case. Choosing uniformly among a variable number of neighbors is generally asymmetric: q(x,y)=1/d(x) and q(y,x)=1/d(y) give the correction d(x)/d(y), where d is vertex degree.[ref]
The useful idea is to separate exploring from insisting on improvement: an uphill move can open a route to a better feasible solution. Its usefulness depends on the proposal distribution, the scale of the objective function, and the cooling schedule for simulated annealing. Finite practical schedules carry no general guarantee of finding a global minimum.

Only adjacent integers are neighbors. At each interior state propose left or right with probability 1/2 each; at an endpoint propose its sole neighbor with probability 1/2 and itself with probability 1/2. This proposal distribution is symmetric, including at the endpoints. The local minimum at 1 is relative to these allowed moves; 4 is the unique global minimum.

Feasible point (x∈F)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
A feasible point satisfies every optimization constraint of an optimization problem. For the budget constraint example, the feasible set is exactly
F={(x,10−x):0≤x≤10}.
(22)
It is the line segment from (0,10) to (10,0), a compact set and a convex set. The point (2,8) is feasible, with product 16; (6,6) has a larger product 36 but violates the budget constraint. Feasibility answers whether a decision is allowed; optimality asks whether any allowed decision is better. The extreme value theorem guarantees that this continuous objective function attains its maximum on this nonempty compact set.
Eliminating y gives a one-variable objective function:
q(x)=x(10−x)=25−(x−5)2,0≤x≤10.
(23)
By completing the square, q(x)≤25, with equality exactly at x=5. Alternatively its derivative is q′(x)=10−2x, which vanishes at 5; the endpoint values are both zero. Completing the square proves global optimality directly, whereas the first-order optimality condition only identifies a candidate. It also quantifies the cost of imbalance: moving to (5+δ,5−δ) with ∣δ∣≤5 loses exactly δ2 units of product. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives another short certificate: xy​≤(x+y)/2=5, with equality exactly when x=y.
For a transportation problem with capacity inequalities, feasibility requires nonnegative shipments, row totals no greater than factory capacities and column totals equal to shop demands. Feasibility alone does not prove minimal cost: a matching transportation dual certificate with capacity inequalities provides an optimality proof. The feasible set can be empty, and a finite infimum need not be attained even when the set is nonempty.

The set of all feasible points of an optimization problem. It depends on the optimization constraints and the decision domain; the objective function ranks its members.
Think of three successive questions. Which decisions can be represented in the model? Which satisfy every optimization constraint? Which of those receive the best objective function value? For decisions z in a domain D, inequalities gi​(z)≤0 and equations hj​(z)=0 define the feasible region
F={z∈D:gi​(z)≤0 for every i, hj​(z)=0 for every j}.
(24)
The domain must be contained in the domain of a function for every function being evaluated; choosing integers rather than real numbers as decisions can also change the feasible set. Constraint satisfaction determines membership of F. Minimizing an objective function f then compares its members by f(z), with optimal value infz∈F​f(z). Changing the scores while keeping D and the optimization constraints fixed leaves F unchanged, provided the new objective function is defined throughout D. These distinctions separate an allowed decision from a best decision.[ref]

Take the decision domain D=R2 and minimize the objective function

Each inequality permits a closed half-space; their intersection is the filled triangle with vertices (0,0), (3,0) and (0,3), including its edges. The feasible region is a compact set and a convex set. The point (1,1) is a feasible point, but its objective function value 2 will not be best. Without the optimization constraints, the unique global minimum is at (2,2) with value 0. That point is infeasible because 2+2>3.
The objective function is the squared Euclidean distance from (2,2). Its positive level sets are circles centered there. Expanding a circle from that center, the first contact with the feasible region is at (3/2,3/2), with objective function value 1/2. Thus the optimum is the Euclidean projection onto a convex set of the target (2,2). Squaring a nonnegative Euclidean distance preserves which point is nearest.[ref]
Here is a direct certificate, without relying on the picture. Put s=x+y and d=x−y. The objective function becomes

Equality requires s=3 and d=0, so the unique optimum is (3/2,3/2). At this point x+y≤3 is an active constraint, while x≥0 and y≥0 are strict. An active constraint identifies a tight restriction at a specified point; it alone does not establish optimality. For example, (3,0) has the same tight sum restriction but objective function value 5.
For a check using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, write the inequalities as −x≤0, −y≤0, g=x+y−3≤0. Their Lagrange multipliers at the optimum are (0,0,1). The gradient equation is

Dynamic programming

Words: 2k Articles: 34
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Dynamic programming solves a mathematical optimization problem by choosing reusable subproblems, recording their value functions, and combining already solved cases through a recurrence relation. Its attraction is that many possible decision histories can share one continuation calculation. A dynamic programming state must retain everything needed to determine the allowed future choices and their rewards. The 0-1 knapsack problem, for example, needs both the available capacity and which items remain available; capacity alone would lose the restriction that each item can be used at most once.
Two ideas explain when this works. Optimal substructure makes an optimal continuation valid inside a larger optimal solution. When subproblems overlap, storing each answer avoids repeated work: memoization computes entries as needed, while a table fills them in dependency order. Start from known base cases. For a problem indexed by increasing size, compute smaller cases first; for a finite sequence of future decisions, work backwards from the terminal reward, as in the Bellman equation. See Bertsekas, MIT lecture 2: optimality and state augmentation.
Consider a 0-1 knapsack problem with item weights (w1​,w2​,w3​)=(2,3,4), item values (v1​,v2​,v3​)=(3,4,5), and capacity 5. Define the value function Vi​(W) to be the largest total item value obtainable from the first i items with total weight at most W. Here i∈{0,1,2,3} and W∈{0,1,2,3,4,5} specify the dynamic programming state. All weights and capacities are nonnegative integers. The empty selection supplies the base case V0​(W)=0. The recurrence relation is
Vi​(W)={Vi−1​(W),max{Vi−1​(W), vi​+Vi−1​(W−wi​)},​W<wi​,W≥wi​.​
(46)
The two candidates skip or take item i. Both use the previous row, so taking item i cannot take that same item again. The condition W≥wi​ prevents a negative remaining capacity; no entry with W<0 is needed. The optimal substructure is concrete: after taking item i, its companions must solve the smaller 0-1 knapsack problem on the first i−1 items with capacity W−wi​. Otherwise replacing them by a better feasible selection would improve the whole selection. Compare [ref]; those notes index the remaining items in the opposite direction.
The full computation is small enough to see at once:
i\W0123​00000​10000​20333​30344​40345​50377​​
(47)
For example, V2​(5)=max{3,4+3}=7 and V3​(5)=max{7,5+0}=7. Choosing the feasible item with largest individual value takes weight 4, earns 5, and leaves capacity 1, which cannot fit another item. This greedy algorithm misses the two-item selection of weights 2 and 3, whose value is 7. This example tests the largest-individual-value rule; choosing by value divided by weight happens to find the optimum here.
The number V3​(5)=7 is the optimal value, while the choices attaining it form a control policy. To reconstruct one optimal selection, start at (3,5). Equality with V2​(5) allows skipping item 3. At (2,5), taking item 2 gives 4+V1​(2)=7, so continue to (1,2). Take item 1 and finish at (0,0). In a tie, either maximizing choice suffices to recover one optimum. Recording choices during the calculation or comparing stored entries afterwards recovers the control policy; a final optimal value alone does not describe the selection.
For n items and integer capacity W≥1, the table uses time complexity O(nW) and space complexity O(nW), counting arithmetic operations and stored numbers using Big O notation. This is pseudo-polynomial time: when weights and capacity use the binary numeral system, the capacity needs only O(log(W+1)) digits. A capacity near 2b creates about 2b columns despite needing only about b digits. Thus this algorithm is practical for moderate capacities but does not establish polynomial time in the encoded input length. See MIT 6.006 recitation 19: knapsack and input size. For the optimal value alone, one array reduces space complexity to O(W): for each item, update capacities in descending order, from W down to wi​. Ascending order would read entries already updated for that item and could reuse it. Reconstruction then requires extra information or recomputation.
The link between the knapsack problem and dynamic programming is already explicit in a 1957 paper by Richard Bellman at RAND: its abstract discusses an exact knapsack problem solution using functional equations and cites his 1957 book. See Bellman, Comment on Dantzig's Paper on Discrete Variable Extremum Problems (1957).

Bellman equation (Vt​(s)=maxa​{rt​(s,a)+Vt+1​(Ft​(s,a))})

Words: 641 Articles: 6
Dynamic programming OurBigBook.com
A Bellman equation expresses the dynamic programming principle as a recurrence relation for a value function: optimize the current reward plus the best attainable continuation. Let s be a dynamic programming state, At​(s) the allowed actions at time t, rt​(s,a) the immediate reward, and Ft​(s,a) the next dynamic programming state. With terminal time T and terminal reward g, the deterministic finite-horizon Bellman equation is
VT​(s)=g(s),Vt​(s)=maxa∈At​(s)​{rt​(s,a)+Vt+1​(Ft​(s,a))},t=T−1,…,0.
(48)
Here Vt​(s) measures total reward from time t through the terminal reward. Start with g and evaluate backwards; the terminal condition anchors the recurrence relation. For finite nonempty action sets, finite rewards, and finite terminal rewards, a maximum exists at each step. If an optimum need not be attained, use a supremum. A minimization problem instead uses a minimum or infimum. The 0-1 knapsack problem above is the same comparison between an immediate item value plus a continuation and the continuation after skipping. See Bertsekas, MIT lecture 2: the backwards recursion.
In a Markov decision process, the next dynamic programming state St+1​ is random. If rt​(s,a) denotes the expected immediate reward and β is a discount factor, the finite-horizon Bellman equation becomes
VT​(s)=g(s),Vt​(s)=maxa∈At​(s)​{rt​(s,a)+βE[Vt+1​(St+1​)∣St​=s, at​=a]}.
(49)
The conditional expectation averages over the next dynamic programming state before choosing the current action; that action cannot use a future outcome that has not yet been observed. For a finite state space with transition probabilities pt​(s′∣s,a), the continuation term is β∑s′​pt​(s′∣s,a)Vt+1​(s′). Taking β=1 gives the undiscounted finite-horizon problem. With a discount factor 0≤β<1, rewards k steps ahead carry a factor βk, including the terminal reward. A maximizing action for each (t,s) specifies a Markov policy, which contains decisions rather than just optimal scores.
For an infinite horizon with a finite state space, finite nonempty action sets, time-independent transition probabilities, bounded rewards ∣r(s,a)∣≤M, and a discount factor 0≤β<1, the optimal value function satisfies
V(s)=maxa∈A(s)​{r(s,a)+β∑s′​p(s′∣s,a)V(s′)},∣V(s)∣≤1−βM​.
(50)
In this setting the maximizing dynamic programming operator is a contraction mapping in the supremum norm, so the Banach fixed-point theorem gives a unique bounded fixed point and convergence of repeated application to it. See Bertsekas, MIT lecture 15: bounded discounted problems. These hypotheses matter: with one state, one action, zero reward, and β=1, the Bellman equation is merely V(s)=V(s), so every finite constant is a fixed point, although the actual total-reward value function is zero. The average-reward Bellman equation and Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation address other settings with their own conditions.

Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions (∇x​L=0,λi​gi​=0)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions combine membership of the feasible set with a balance of gradients and complementary slackness. For a minimization problem with differentiable functions on an open subset of Rn, write
minx​f(x),gi​(x)≤0 (1≤i≤m),hj​(x)=0 (1≤j≤p),
(56)
and use the optimization Lagrangian
L(x,λ,μ)=f(x)+∑i=1m​λi​gi​(x)+∑j=1p​μj​hj​(x).
(57)
A candidate (x∗​,λ,μ) satisfies the KKT conditions exactly when all four requirements hold:
  • Primal feasibility: gi​(x∗​)≤0 and hj​(x∗​)=0, so x∗​ is a feasible point.
  • Dual sign feasibility: λi​≥0. The equality Lagrange multipliers μj​ are unrestricted real numbers.
  • Stationarity: the gradient of the optimization Lagrangian in the decision variables vanishes,
    ∇x​L(x∗​,λ,μ)=∇f(x∗​)+∑i​λi​∇gi​(x∗​)+∑j​μj​∇hj​(x∗​)=0.
    (58)
  • Complementary slackness: λi​gi​(x∗​)=0 for every inequality optimization constraint.[ref]
The sign of each inequality Lagrange multiplier follows the chosen convention gi​≤0: on the feasible set, λi​gi​≤0 makes the optimization Lagrangian a lower bound on the objective function. An equality contributes zero on the feasible set for either sign of its Lagrange multiplier. Complementary slackness says an inequality with gi​(x∗​)<0 must have λi​=0, while λi​>0 implies an active constraint. An active constraint can still have zero Lagrange multiplier; the quadratic minimization with a moving upper bound below gives an explicit example.
The name records William Karush's 1939 master's thesis and the 1951 work of Harold W. Kuhn and Albert W. Tucker.[ref]

KKT regularity at a local minimum

Words: 202
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions OurBigBook.com
At a local minimum of continuously differentiable functions, a suitable constraint qualification guarantees the existence of Lagrange multipliers satisfying the KKT conditions. One sufficient local regularity assumption is that the gradients of the equality optimization constraints and the active constraints are jointly linearly independent. This assumption concerns the description of the feasible set, not just the smoothness of the objective function.[ref]
To see why a hypothesis is needed, minimize f(x)=x subject to g(x)=x2≤0. The feasible set is the singleton {0}, so x∗​=0 is a global minimum. Yet f′(0)+λg′(0)=1 for every finite Lagrange multiplier λ. Thus this convex optimization problem has an attained optimum without a KKT multiplier. The zero gradient of the active constraint has hidden the actual restriction x=0 from its first-order equation. Rewriting it as the equality h(x)=x=0 yields the unrestricted Lagrange multiplier μ=−1.
For convex optimization, Slater's condition requires strict inequalities and affine equalities at a point in the relative interior of the common domain of a function. A finite optimum value then gives strong duality and dual attainment. Primal attainment and differentiability yield KKT multipliers. Affine inequalities may be nonstrict in the refined version.[ref]
Slater's condition is sufficient, and need not hold for an optimum to exist. The singular example above also shows that mere primal attainment is not a substitute for a constraint qualification.

Convex KKT optimality certificate (f(x∗​)≤f(z)(z feasible))

Words: 196
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions OurBigBook.com
For differentiable functions f,gi​ that are convex functions on an open convex set and affine functions hj​, the KKT conditions certify a global minimum. Once Lagrange multipliers satisfy them, no extra Slater condition is needed.[ref]
The certificate is a short chain of inequalities. Nonnegative Lagrange multipliers and affine equalities make L(⋅,λ,μ) a convex function. Its zero gradient gives a global minimum at x∗​ by the first-order optimality condition. For every feasible point z,
f(x∗​)=L(x∗​,λ,μ)≤L(z,λ,μ)≤f(z).
(59)
The first equality uses feasibility and complementary slackness; the last inequality uses gi​(z)≤0 and λi​≥0. Equivalently, the Lagrange dual function attains the same value as the primal objective function, proving strong duality. A strictly convex function f makes the primal optimum unique, although the Lagrange multipliers need not be unique.
Affine equality optimization constraints matter: an arbitrary signed multiple of a nonlinear equality can destroy convexity of the optimization Lagrangian. For example, minimizing (x−2)2 subject to the affine equality x=b gives x∗​=b and μ=2(2−b) for L=(x−2)2+μ(x−b). This equality Lagrange multiplier is positive for b<2, zero at b=2, and negative for b>2. Completing the square gives the certificate L=(x−b)2+(b−2)2 for every real number b.
Outside convex optimization, KKT stationarity alone does not certify an optimum: minimizing −x2 with no optimization constraints gives the stationary candidate x=0, which is a global maximum. The Lagrangian sufficiency theorem remains applicable whenever a global minimum of the optimization Lagrangian can be proved directly.

The objective function is a strictly convex function with its unconstrained optimization minimum at x=2. If b<2, it decreases throughout the feasible set until the bound x=b is reached. If b≥2, the feasible set already contains 2. Hence
x∗​(b)=min(2,b),V(b)=(max(2−b,0))2.
(61)
With g(x)=x−b, the optimization Lagrangian and KKT conditions are
L=(x−2)2+λ(x−b),x≤b,λ≥0,2(x−2)+λ=0,λ(x−b)=0.
(62)
Substituting x∗​(b) gives the unique inequality Lagrange multiplier
λ∗​(b)=2max(2−b,0).

For b<2, the active constraint has λ∗​>0. For b>2, there is strict slack b−x∗​=b−2 and λ∗​=0. At b=2, the active constraint has zero Lagrange multiplier: the boundary happens to pass through the unconstrained optimum. Feasibility and complementary slackness must both be checked; solving only 2(x−2)+λ=0 would allow infeasible candidates.
An independent certificate follows by completing the square:
L=(x−2+2λ​)2+λ(2−b)−4λ2​,db​(λ)=infx∈R​L=λ(2−b)−4λ2​.
(64)
The Lagrange dual function is a concave function of λ. Its maximum over λ≥0 occurs at λ∗​(b) and equals V(b). Thus every case has an explicit lower bound attained by a feasible point; the KKT conditions provide a certificate that can be checked without searching all real numbers.

Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions OurBigBook.com
A shadow price measures the marginal improvement from relaxing an inequality optimization constraint. Use L=f+∑i​λi​(gi​−bi​)+∑j​μj​hj​ for gi​(x)≤bi​ in a minimization problem. With strong duality and a differentiable optimal value function, ∂V/∂bi​=−λi​.[ref]

V′(b)={−2(2−b),0,​b<2,b≥2,​V′(b)=−λ∗​(b).

The derivative at b=2 is zero from both sides, although x∗​(b) has different one-sided derivatives there. The value of additional room has faded continuously to zero just as the active constraint stops restricting the optimizer.
At b=1, x∗​=1, V=1 and λ∗​=2. Raising the bound to 1.1 lowers the value to 0.81: the first-order prediction is a change of −2(0.1)=−0.2, while the exact change is −0.19. There is also a global statement in this example. Keeping the Lagrange multiplier at the value associated with b0​, the Lagrange dual function changes by −λ∗​(b0​)(b−b0​). Weak duality therefore gives

If the value function is not differentiable, an optimal Lagrange multiplier can instead supply a supporting subgradient, rather than a unique marginal rate. This is the same idea used in sensitivity analysis in convex perturbation duality.

Unconstrained optimization

Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
Optimization with no additional optimization constraints on the chosen variable domain. At an interior local extremum of a differentiable function, the first-order optimality condition is ∇f=0.

Lagrange multiplier (λ)

Words: 2k Articles: 16
Mathematical optimization OurBigBook.com
For continuously differentiable functions f,g on an open subset of Rn, suppose z∗​ is a local extremum of f subject to g(z)=b, with ∇g(z∗​)=0. Then a real number λ, the Lagrange multiplier, satisfies
∇f(z∗​)=λ∇g(z∗​).
(67)
The nonzero gradient assumption excludes singular points of the optimization constraint. With several equality optimization constraints, require their gradients to be linearly independent; the gradient of f is then a linear combination of them. These are necessary conditions, not automatic certificates of a global maximum or global minimum.
Why can the gradient be nonzero at an optimum? In unconstrained optimization, every direction is available at an interior local extremum, so all directional derivatives vanish and ∇f=0. On a regular equality feasible set, only directions in its tangent space are available to first order. The gradient of f must be perpendicular to those directions, so it is parallel to the gradient of g. In two dimensions this explains the tangency of their level sets. See MIT, Lagrange multipliers and contour geometry.
For the product example, set g(x,y)=x+y and use the optimization Lagrangian
L(x,y,λ)=xy−λ(x+y−10).
(68)
Its partial derivatives give y−λ=0, x−λ=0, and x+y=10. Hence x=y=λ=5. At (5,5), ∇f=(5,5)=5(1,1)=λ∇g: increasing both inputs would help, but is infeasible. Along the allowed direction (1,−1), the directional derivative is zero. The endpoints must still be checked because of the nonnegativity optimization constraints; completing the square establishes the unique global maximum.
The sign convention matters: writing L=xy+μ(x+y−10) instead gives μ=−5. Neither equality Lagrange multiplier has a universal nonnegativity requirement. Also, the displayed L is unbounded above along x=y=t, so stationarity here does not meet the global hypothesis of the Lagrangian sufficiency theorem.
The Lagrange multiplier also measures the value of extra resources. For a positive budget b, the optimizer is (b/2,b/2), the optimum value is V(b)=b2/4, and V′(b)=b/2=λ. At b=10, an extra 0.1 units predicts a gain of 0.5; the exact gain is V(10.1)−V(10)=0.5025. This is the envelope theorem in a computed sensitivity analysis: the multiplier translates a binding budget constraint into a marginal benefit.

Lagrange multiplier OurBigBook.com
A rigid stick of negligible width can turn horizontally between perpendicular corridors of widths a,b>0 precisely when its length does not exceed the displayed value, allowing contact with the walls. A position touching the two outer walls and the inner corner has endpoint intercepts (a+X,0) and (0,b+Y) with X,Y>0. Collinearity with the inner corner (a,b) is equivalent to XY=ab.
Minimize the squared intercept length F=(a+X)2+(b+Y)2 under this optimization constraint. The Lagrange multiplier equations imply X(a+X)=Y(b+Y). Substituting Y=ab/X gives (X3−ab2)(X+a)=0, so the admissible point is X=(ab2)1/3, Y=(a2b)1/3. There F=(a2/3+b2/3)3. Along the positive constraint branch F tends to infinity at both ends and has this one stationary point, proving it is the minimum available clearance over orientations. That minimum is the maximum stick length which can pass through every intermediate orientation.

Suppose two adjustable inputs must deliver a prescribed total c, and their combined cost is the quadratic form f(x,y)=x2+2y2. These are chosen, dimensionless quantities; the coefficient 2 makes concentrating an input in y more expensive. Initially allow all real numbers x,y, with the equality optimization constraint g(x,y)=x+y=c. The optimization Lagrangian with our chosen sign is
L=x2+2y2−λ(x+y−c).

x∗​=32c​,y∗​=3c​,λ∗​=34c​,V(c)=32c2​.​

For c=3, the unique global minimum is at (2,1), with cost 6 and Lagrange multiplier 4. Equal allocation would cost 6.75; assigning everything to x would cost 9. At the optimum, the two marginal costs agree: ∂x​f=∂y​f=4. Moving a little input from one component to the other therefore has zero first-order effect on cost. When c>0, this solution also meets the extra nonnegativity optimization constraints x,y≥0, so it remains optimal with those added.
Here the Lagrange multiplier equations locate a candidate, and a short independent check certifies it. On the entire feasible set, substitute y=c−x and use completing the square:
x2+2(c−x)2=3(x−32c​)2+32c2​.

The squared term is nonnegative and vanishes only at x=2c/3. Thus the candidate is the unique global minimum; there is no global maximum on this unbounded feasible set, a line. This separates finding a stationary point from proving optimality. The geometric beauty is that equal marginal costs, parallel gradients, tangency of level sets, and completing the square identify the same allocation.
